newsitem.title: FRANCE: Former south France godfather-politican on trial.
newsitem.headline: Former south France godfather-politican on trial.

text.p: The former political boss of the Var department of southern France, Maurice Arreckx, who liked to describe himself as "the Godfather," goes to court on Monday in the latest of France's recurrent political corruption trials.
Arreckx, 79, the area's representative to the French senate when arrested in August 1994, is accused of seeking a two million franc ($400,000) kickback on a public works construction contract.

Similar trials have become increasingly common in the French political world but the Arreckx case has drawn special attention because of his reputed past ties with local gangland chief Jean-Louis Fargette who has since been murdered.
Investigators have told reporters Fargette publicly claimed Arreckx "swindled" him out of a cut in the kickback money.

The Var has been under the spotlight since 1993 when local parliamentarian Yann Piat, like Arreckx a member of the centre-rightist Union for French Democracy (UDF) party, was also killed after she threatened to reveal "Mafia-like" activities in the region.

But the latest case cuts across party lines since one of five other people on trial with Arreckx is a former local Socialist regional councillor accused of being a contact between the ex-senator and Fargette.

Arreckx was conditionally released from jail for health reasons in May 1995 pending trial. He initially claimed the funds he partly received in a Swiss bank account were for his UDF party which he claimed had "sacrificed" him.
Arreckx was long-time mayor of the Mediterranean port of Toulon which anti-crime campaigners claim is one of the most corruption-ridden in France.
They say they suspect the area is also used as a clearing house for funds from the Mafia operating across the nearby Italian border.

Wide-scale political corruption has become a major problem in France over the past two decades as a result of the central Paris government devolving many of its powers and budgets to locally-elected regional authorities.

The aim of the policy was to allow local residents more control over decisions affecting their everyday lives which, since the Emperor Napoleon, were taken in Paris by faceless, but apparently incorruptible, bureaucrats.
But the decentralisation also opened the gates to widespread "deals" in which local politicians demanded kickbacks in exchange for approving regional or municipal contracts.

Another top southern political figure, Cannes Mayor Michel Mouillot, is currently in jail for seeking such a kickback from a British casino chain in exchange for permission to set up an establishment in his resort city.
The mayors of Nice, Lyon and Grenoble have all been embroiled in similar cases.

One of the most explosive cases now examined by magistrates involves Paris mayor Jean Tiberi because many of the suspected offences in the capital may have had their roots during the time when Paris's mayor was Jacques Chirac, who was elected president of France last year.
